passages.happening:
‘This is the burden that Habakkuk the prophet received in a vision’ (verse 1). He cries to God: ‘How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear’ (verse 2)? He cries out about violence, and God does not save. ‘Why do You make me see iniquity? Why do You tolerate wrongdoing?’ (verse 3). Destruction and violence are before him, and strife is everywhere.

‘Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth. For the wicked hem in the righteous, so that justice is perverted’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The injustice of these verses fits Judah after King Josiah died in 609 BC. His son Jehoiakim reversed much of his father's reform, and Jeremiah condemned him for building his palace by injustice.

Habakkuk uses the language of Israel's law courts. The law, torah, God's instruction, is paralyzed or numb, and justice never goes out, because the courts that should protect the righteous are surrounded and bent by the wicked. For Habakkuk's hearers justice was not an idea but the daily business of elders and judges at the city gate.

He speaks in the form of a lament, familiar from the psalms: an address to God, the question how long, and a description of distress. He does not pretend that all is well, and he takes his complaint to God.
passages.later: The psalms ask the same question: ‘How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?’ (Psalm 13:1). Jeremiah condemned Jehoiakim: ‘Woe to him who builds his palace by unrighteousness’ (Jeremiah 22:13).
passages.asks: Habakkuk asks God how long, and why. Ask whether you have ever been afraid to bring God your honest questions. And ask what injustice you see that you have stopped complaining to God about.

passages.happening:
God answers. Habakkuk is to look at the nations and be astounded, for ‘I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe even if someone told you’ (verse 5). ‘For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans’ (verse 6), a ruthless and impetuous nation that marches across the earth to seize homes that are not theirs.

They are dreaded and feared, and they make their own law (verse 7). Their horses are swifter than leopards and fiercer than wolves at evening, and they swoop like a vulture (verse 8). They come bent on violence and gather prisoners like sand (verse 9). They mock kings and laugh at every fortress (verse 10). ‘They are guilty; their own strength is their god’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The Chaldeans were first tribes in southern Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. In 626 BC a Chaldean leader, Nabopolassar, seized Babylon and founded the empire historians call Neo-Babylonian. With the Medes, Babylon destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, and under his son Nebuchadnezzar it defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC and became master of the region, Judah included.

The chapter describes that rise as if it had not yet been fully felt: God says he is doing a work people would not believe, which fits a time before Babylon's power was obvious. The pictures are of terror: horses faster than leopards, wolves hunting at evening, a vulture swooping, and siege ramps heaped against fortress walls, a standard method of Mesopotamian warfare.

God's answer to Habakkuk's complaint about injustice is judgment. But the last line already looks ahead: these conquerors are guilty, and their strength is their god.
passages.later: Paul quoted verse 5 in his sermon at Pisidian Antioch, warning his hearers: ‘For I am doing a work in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you’ (Acts 13:41).
passages.asks: God's answer to Habakkuk was not what he expected. Ask how you respond when God's answer to your prayer is harder than the problem. And ask what you trust as your strength.

passages.t: How can a holy God use them?
passages.happening:
Habakkuk asks again. ‘Are You not from everlasting, O LORD, my God, my Holy One?’ (verse 12). God has appointed the Chaldeans to judge and correct. ‘Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil, and You cannot tolerate wrongdoing. So why do You tolerate the faithless?’ (verse 13). Why is he silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?

People are like fish in the sea (verse 14). The conqueror pulls them up with a hook and gathers them in his net, and rejoices (verse 15). He sacrifices to his net and burns incense to it, because it makes him rich (verse 16). Will he keep emptying his net and killing nations without mercy (verse 17)?
passages.hearers:
Habakkuk's second complaint is built on a contrast between who God is, from everlasting, holy, the Rock, too pure to look on evil, and what God seems to allow. Verse 12 contains a line saying that they will not die, which Jewish scribal tradition lists among a few places where scribes are said to have changed a phrase out of reverence for God.

The fishing picture draws on common practice. Hooks, dragnets and casting nets were used on the Nile and in the rivers and marshes of Mesopotamia. The conqueror treats people as a catch, and worships the tools of his success. The complaint runs on into 2:1, where Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower.
passages.later: Isaiah too called Assyria the rod of God's anger, and then announced judgment on its arrogance (Isaiah 10:5-12). Jeremiah pictured God sending fishermen to catch his people (Jeremiah 16:16).
passages.hard:
How can God use a nation more wicked than Judah to punish Judah?

This is Habakkuk's own question, and the book takes it seriously. Scripture gives several answers. God's use of a nation does not mean he approves of it: Isaiah calls Assyria the rod of God's anger and then announces judgment on Assyria for its arrogance, and Habakkuk 2 does the same for Babylon. The judgment on Judah was not arbitrary; the prophets had warned for generations that unfaithfulness to the covenant would bring exile. And God's rule of history works through free human agents, who remain responsible for their cruelty even when their actions serve a larger purpose.

Some readers find these answers enough. Others think the Bible leaves a remainder of mystery, which is why God's reply in chapter 2 calls for faith and patience rather than giving a full explanation. What the chapter refuses is the easy answer that God does not care or is not there. It gives no one a way to read a particular people's suffering, then or now, as God's verdict.
passages.asks: Habakkuk holds on to who God is while asking why God allows what he sees. Ask what you know of God that you can stand on when you do not understand what he is doing. And ask what tools of success you have been tempted to worship.
